title: Robert Eggers' 'Werwulf' Promises His Darkest Film Yet — Plus an Interactive Game
summary:
Fall is in the air, and that means a new Robert Eggers movie can't be far behind. The director behind "The Witch," "The Lighthouse," "The Northman," and "Nosferatu" is bringing his Gothic sensibilities to another classic monster this December with "Werwulf."

The lycanthropy saga — that's the fancy word for werewolf stories — is set in an English village in the 13th century. Aaron Taylor-Johnson stars as a man who undergoes terrifying transformations into a werewolf each full moon. Plot details remain scarce, but Eggers fans can expect stunning production design, period-appropriate language, and performances from his trusted ensemble, including Willem Dafoe and Lily Rose-Depp.

Focus Features previously screened footage at CinemaCon before releasing the film's first trailer. Now the studio has shared a second trailer that offers a closer look. During a conversation on the Universal lot, Eggers teased that the film is the darkest of his career — no small feat.

"You're always trying to push yourself and challenge yourself," Eggers said. "And after 'Nosferatu,' I kind of said, 'Let me try to write the scariest thing I can write.' I don't know that I did that, but I definitely wrote the darkest thing."

He explained that the idea came from historical werewolf accounts he'd read since high school. "They were doing things that were so taboo and hard for anyone to wrap their mind around because it was so extreme that the culture that they existed in said, 'You can't be a human, you must be a werewolf.' So it was going to be very dark and very primal subject matter."

"Werwulf" is written by Eggers and frequent collaborator Sjón. The official synopsis reads: "A harrowing tale of devotion, damnation, and the devil within." It's in theaters Friday, December 25 — and there's an interactive game for fans to try now.
why_it_matters: Horror like this is a window into how earlier societies explained violence, outsiders and forbidden desires — the werewolf trials were really about communities deciding who counted as human. Its release strategy also shows how modern studios now build hype with trailers and interactive games rather than posters alone.

background_read: Robert Eggers is an American director known for slow, atmospheric horror built on real folklore and history. His first film, 'The Witch,' followed a Puritan family in colonial New England; 'The Lighthouse' and 'The Northman' pushed further into myth and Viking history; and 'Nosferatu' was his remake of a century-old vampire classic.

Werewolf stories are among the oldest monster tales in Europe. In parts of medieval and early modern Europe, people were actually put on trial as werewolves, accused of making a pact with the devil — the kind of historical record Eggers says he has been reading since high school.

Aaron Taylor-Johnson (a British actor) and Willem Dafoe (an American actor and longtime Eggers collaborator) star, while Sjón — an Icelandic poet and novelist who also writes lyrics — co-wrote the script.

Focus Features is the studio releasing the film, and CinemaCon is a yearly convention in Las Vegas where studios show early footage to cinema owners. Eggers's films are also known for period-accurate dialogue, which some viewers find harder to follow than ordinary modern speech.

perspectives.description: Eggers delivers exactly what his audience wants: meticulous period detail, strange old language, and a returning cast. Calling it his darkest film yet is exciting rather than worrying for viewers who loved 'The Witch' and 'Nosferatu'.

Studios routinely claim each new horror film is the scariest or darkest one yet, and with plot details kept scarce it is hard to judge anything beyond the trailers. The interactive game may be doing more work than the story itself.

Monster films keep returning to medieval folklore because those stories record real social fears. Werewolf accusations were a way of expelling people the community considered dangerous, so a film about them is really about exclusion and belief, not just transformation.

A Christmas Day release plus a companion game suggests studios are testing transmedia marketing for auteur horror. If it works, more directors may get bigger budgets — and more pressure to turn their films into franchises.
